name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm sixty hectares on the Mill Road that were my father's, plus thirty I rent for grazing. Forty beef cattle and eight hectares of potatoes, which go to a packer in town. In winter I go hedge-cutting for other farms with my tractor and flail, which brings in a fair bit. The day is feeding, fencing, and in season, the potato harvester breaking down at the worst moment.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Marta works three days a week at the bank branch in town, doing loans and accounts. Our two boys are grown: Tiago's a mechanic and Bruno's in the police. I've got a phone that makes calls, and that suits me. Marta does anything on the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say anyway: let's see. Most of these big promises come to nothing. At the potato packer's yard, that's what everyone would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the potato price is my worry, AI or not. The packer cut the contract price last year, and the bank where Marta works has already closed two branches in the county. We've a few months saved, and that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, but tighter. I'd cancel the plan to replace the potato harvester and patch the old one again. I'd take on two more farms for winter hedge-cutting, which is cash in hand when the potatoes pay badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of the computers, because of the packer and the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Marta's branch closed, what would happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be offered the branch in the next town, forty minutes away, and she'd probably take it. That's more diesel and less time, but it's still a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new kitchen she wants. I know, I know. But a potato harvester breaking down in October costs more than a new kitchen.

say: Let's **see**: most big promises **come to nothing** in the end.
That's what everyone at the **packer's yard** would say, without a second thought.
think: The **potato price** worries him more than any AI.
Marta's **bank branch** could close, and they have only a few months saved.
do: Patch the **old harvester** again instead of replacing it.
Take on **two more farms** for winter hedge-cutting.
Put off the **new kitchen** at home.
feel: **Uneasy** about the packer and the bank, not the computers.
S0.quote: A potato harvester breaking down in October costs more than a new kitchen.
fieldNote: His pressures are the **packer's price** and his wife's **bank job**, both already there.
Doesn't use AI at all and doesn't plan to; he talks about **diesel and parts**.
Pragmatic: cuts where it hurts least and adds **hedge-cutting** income.

steps.text: Patch the old potato harvester instead of buying a new one
Put off the new kitchen at home
Take on two more farms for winter hedge-cutting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard on the office workers, and I'd mean it. At the mart I'd say farming's safe for now. Online I wouldn't say anything, because I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one that gets Marta. Loans, accounts, answering customers, that's her whole job. If her three days go to two or none, we lose about a third of what comes into the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Marta and put a fixed amount into savings every month, starting now, before anything happens. I'd chase more hedge-cutting and maybe some potato contract work for neighbours. And I'd tell her not to wait for the bank to decide, but to ask about redundancy terms early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, mostly for her. She's good at what she does, and it doesn't feel fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning any of these tools for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Marta does the forms, and if she's home more, she'd do them faster. I'm fifty-eight and I'd rather be on the tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marta that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Marta that the farm's paid for and we'll eat, then lie awake doing the sums.

say: It's going to be **hard on office workers**.
Farming's **safe for now**, as he'd say at the mart.
think: Marta's **bank job** is exactly what this replaces.
Losing her days means losing about **a third** of household income.
do: Put a **fixed sum** into savings every month, starting now.
Chase more **hedge-cutting** and potato contract work.
Urge Marta to ask about **redundancy terms** early.
feel: **Worried** for Marta, and a sense that it's **not fair**.
S1.quote: I'd tell my wife Marta that the farm's paid for and we'll eat, then lie awake doing the sums.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption hits his household through **Marta's desk job**, not his farm.
Stays **resistant** to tools himself, even while the risk is real.
His answer is **cash**: savings and more contract work.

steps.text: Save a fixed amount every month with Marta, starting now
Find more hedge-cutting and potato contract work for neighbours
Cut household spending to cover a possible loss of Marta's days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and that the government had better have a plan. I'm not one for big speeches, but I'd say it at the packer's and at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Marta's job goes in 2028, straight away. Then by 2031 the robots come for hands-on work, and the big farms get robot harvesters and robot hedge-cutters. My winter money goes, the potato price drops, and I'm sixty-one with a third of our income already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't feed, diesel or the mortgage on the grazing land. I'd sell the hedge-cutting flail while it still fetches a price, maybe eight thousand. And I'd probably sell the thirty-hectare grazing lease back to the landlord and shrink to what I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's moving. I don't sleep well picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes three years before the robots. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta goes first and I go second, then the robots take my extra money too. That's three years of me working harder to cover her wage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask anyone for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Bruno has offered before, and I said no. I'd probably have to say yes this time, and I'd hate it. Maybe whatever the government puts on, if there's anything.

say: Nobody's **ready**, and the government had better have **a plan**.
He'd say it at the **packer's** and the **mart**, not in speeches.
think: Marta's job goes in **2028**, and robots take his **winter work** by 2031.
At sixty-one, a **third of income** is already gone before the robots.
do: Cut everything but **feed, diesel** and the land mortgage.
Sell the **hedge-cutting flail** while it's worth about eight thousand.
Give up the **thirty-hectare** grazing lease and shrink to what he owns.
feel: Like the **ground is moving**; he doesn't **sleep** well.
S2.quote: Marta goes first and I go second, then the robots take my extra money too.
fieldNote: The three-year gap means **two hits** in a row: his wife's wage, then his contract income.
Responds by **shrinking**, not investing; avoids risk to the end.
Would accept help from son **Bruno** only under pressure.

steps.text: Cut spending to feed, diesel and the land mortgage only
Sell the hedge-cutting flail while it still fetches about eight thousand
Hand the thirty-hectare grazing lease back to the landlord
Accept son Bruno's offer of money if it comes to that

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get ready if they're told straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would be sixty-three in 2031, near enough to stop anyway, so losing her job hurts less. The robots in 2034 come when I'm sixty-six. The farm's mine, so I'd still have it, just less money from the extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder now, while we've both got work. I'd stop renting the extra grazing in about 2033 and slim the herd to what our own land carries. Otherwise I'd wait and see what the robots actually do before deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. It's still our money shrinking, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the potato packer buys from robot farms only, I'd stop the potatoes and keep just the cattle. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Tiago, the mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tiago to learn to fix the robots, because somebody will have to. He'd tell me he's already on it.

say: Five years is **something**, at least, compared with the fast one.
People can get ready if they're **told straight** about what's coming.
think: Marta would be near **stopping** anyway by 2031.
Robots in **2034** come at sixty-six; the land is his, but **extra income** shrinks.
do: Save harder **now** while both still have work.
Wait and see what the **robots really do** before deciding more.
feel: **Anxious**, but less than the fast scenario.
S3.quote: If the potato packer buys from robot farms only, I'd stop the potatoes and keep just the cattle.
fieldNote: Five years lines up the losses with **retirement**, softening them.
His household income still **shrinks**, which keeps him anxious.
Typical of him: **wait and see**, with a clear trigger for acting.

steps.text: Save harder now while both still have work
Stop renting the extra grazing around 2033
Wait to see what robots do before changing the potatoes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change. That's what my father would have said, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's after my time, mostly. Marta's retired by 2036, I'm near seventy when the robots come. I'd still have the potato price to grumble about, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep the herd, keep the potatoes while the packer pays. I'd let the hedge-cutting wind down as my back goes. I wouldn't buy anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the normal amount. The packer and the weather, same as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans for the farm itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The boys don't want it, so it'll be sold or rented when I stop. Robots or not, that's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson's only six, and I've no idea what to tell him about leaving school into all this. Ten years goes fast.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and plenty can change before then.
His **father** would have said exactly the same about any new thing.
think: It's mostly **after his time**: Marta's retired and robots come near seventy.
The **potato price** stays his everyday grumble.
do: Keep the **herd and potatoes** while the packer pays.
Let the **hedge-cutting** wind down as his back goes.
feel: The **normal** unease about the packer and the weather.
S4.quote: My grandson's only six, and I've no idea what to tell him about leaving school into all this.
fieldNote: With a decade, his own income is **mostly safe** until he stops.
Plans to **sell or rent** the farm regardless, since his sons don't want it.
His soft spot is his **grandson**, whom he can't advise.

steps.text: Keep the herd and potatoes while the packer pays
Let the winter hedge-cutting wind down as his back goes
Wait and decide on selling or renting the farm nearer seventy

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marta and I both get hit inside three years. What would help is a fair price for potatoes, honestly, and some kind of pension top-up for people who lose work in their sixties. Not courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farm being paid for. That's the only reason I'm not panicking: owning the land means we'll always have somewhere to live and something to eat.

headlineQuote: Owning the land means we'll always have somewhere to live and something to eat.
portrait: Rafael, **58**, owns sixty hectares of beef and **potatoes** and cuts hedges in winter.
He never uses AI; his wife **Marta**, who works at a bank, handles anything digital.
Steady Disruption worries him through **Marta's desk job**, about a third of their income.
In fast AGI he expects **two hits** and responds by shrinking and selling equipment.
Owning the land is his **floor**; he waits and sees when time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Marta's job and his winter **income** gone within three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair potato price** and a pension **top-up** for people losing work in their sixties.
